html:
The Six-Day War was a short war in June 1967 between Israel and its Arab neighbours, mainly Egypt, Syria and Jordan. In six days Israel took the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.

Tension had built for years: border clashes with Syria, Palestinian raids, and quarrels over water, including Israeli strikes on Arab works to divert the Jordan's headwaters away from Israel's National Water Carrier. In May 1967 Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser moved troops into Sinai, sent away the UN peacekeepers and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping.

On 5 June Israel struck first, destroying most of Egypt's air force on the ground within hours. Its army then crossed Sinai to the Suez Canal. Jordan joined the war and lost the West Bank and the old city of Jerusalem. In the last days Israel took the Golan Heights from Syria.

The war changed the Middle East:

  • Some 300,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from the West Bank and Gaza, many for the second time after 1948.
  • Israel began a long occupation and, later, building settlements.
  • Nasser's prestige and Arab nationalism were badly hurt. UN Resolution 242 called for land in exchange for peace.

Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973 to win back their land. Egypt regained Sinai through a peace treaty in 1979; much of the rest is still disputed.
sum: The Six-Day War was a short war in June 1967 between Israel and its Arab neighbours, mainly Egypt, Syria and Jordan. In six days Israel took the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.
